episodes.title: If You Can't Play With Caleb Wilson, You Can't Play for the Bulls with CHGO's Big DAVE
episodes.description:
Chicago Bulls fans are allowed to feel something again — and this time it isn’t blind hope.In this episode of the Hoopsology Podcast, CHGO’s Big DAVE comes on to break down why the 2026-27 Bulls finally feel different. After years of dysfunction and a 31-51 season that missed the playoffs for a fourth straight year, the franchise hit rock bottom… and then started acting like it.The turning point? Michael Reinsdorf looking Bulls Nation in the eye and saying the words fans never expected: “I’m sorry. We screwed up. And I will make this right.” Big Dave says that apology didn’t just land — it healed something in long-suffering fans.From there, the rebuild gets real:

Bryson Graham as the new basketball ops lead — the guy who says if he’s the smartest person in the room, the Bulls will fail
Tiago Splitter as head coach (Popovich tree) + Taj Gibson back on the bench
A bigger player-development staff, more video work, and real collaboration upstairs
An open practice at Horner Park — free, public, never-been-done fan access in Chicago
And then there’s Caleb Wilson.Big Dave is all-in. Wilson’s summer-league work ethic, the “yeah, I’m next” look at the Jordan statue, the record-setting game where he only cared that they lost, and Kevin Garnett showing up just to watch him — none of it feels fluky. Dave’s line is blunt: if you can’t play with Caleb Wilson, you can’t play for the Chicago Bulls.This isn’t “title or bust” hype. It’s logical optimism — a “fun bad” year full of blocks, run-outs, alley-oops, and a roster where everybody has something to prove. Giddey, Powell, Claxton, Patrick Williams, the young pieces… the proving ground is open.🏀 Subscribe to Hoopsology for smart, insider-level NBA and WNBA conversations every week.

episodes.title: Jamal Murray on the Pressure: "I Welcome It"
episodes.description:
The Denver Nuggets are done making excuses. At the 2026 Nuggets Media Day, Aaron Gordon and Jamal Murray got honest about last season's collapse, what it takes to get back to the title, and how a new-look roster changes everything.In this episode of the Hoopsology Podcast, we break down everything they said. Aaron Gordon opened up about the "soul-searching" summer — reading, writing, and traveling to "bring my nervous system back down to regular" — and why, at this stage of his career, "the best ability is availability." 

He pushed back hard on the idea that Denver lost its edge: "I don't think we lost it. We had a lot of injuries last year… but at some point you need your whole team to win a championship."Jamal Murray was just as blunt about the mindset. He talked about loving the game, refusing to be "subpar," and the danger of complacency: "there is a certain level of complacency that comes with mastery. We're fighting that." 

Asked about carrying a heavier load, he didn't flinch — "I enjoyed taking on those challenges, so I welcome it."

We also cover the DeMar DeRozan addition (Gordon: "I was happy we have another 50-point scorer on the team"), how the starting five will adjust the pace, spacing, and those one-handed Jokić lobs for new pieces like Lonnie and Cam, why transition defense is a focus with more athletes on the floor, and how Gordon shut down the online trade rumors — "it's just static, it's just noise."

🏀 Subscribe to Hoopsology for smart, insider-level NBA and WNBA conversations every week.
💬 Are the Nuggets still title favorites in the West? Drop your take in the comments.#DenverNuggets #AaronGordon #JamalMurray

episodes.title: The WNBA Needs Its David Stern — Who's Next in Charge?
episodes.description:
Cathy Engelbert is out as WNBA commissioner — and on this In The Lab clip, the Hoopsology panel breaks down whether she left on her own terms or got pushed out. The verdict? It's complicated.

On the business side, her tenure was historic: team valuations climbed an average of $460 million (some approaching $1 billion), ESPN viewership jumped 17% (1.4M viewers), CBS rose 9%, and she helped negotiate a landmark media rights deal that set the stage for the league's biggest era yet.

But the panel doesn't hold back on the other side of the ledger — the strained player relations that may have cost her the job. A'ja Wilson reportedly barely spoke to her, there was no real relationship with Caitlin Clark, and the delayed Caitlin Clark signature shoe is called out as a marketing fumble that left serious money on the table.

So who's next? We debate the qualities the next commissioner needs — player-friendly AND business-savvy, someone willing to "lay down the law" like David Stern — and float the names in the mix: Swin Cash, Mark Tatum, Sue Bird, and Shareef Abdur-Rahim. Plus: how the league handles rivals like Unrivaled, expansion (Toronto Tempo, Portland Fire), and the push for mainstream legitimacy.

episodes.title: His Favorite Call Ever Was When He Kept His Mouth Shut  Nets Radio Analyst Tim Capstraw
episodes.description:
Tim Capstraw has been the voice next to the Brooklyn Nets for 25 years — and he still can’t believe they’re letting him hang around.In this episode of the Hoopsology Podcast, the Nets radio analyst opens up about the biggest thrill of his life: his first NBA broadcast with the Jason Kidd-era New Jersey Nets, the three weeks of 5 a.m. prep, and the imposter syndrome of a guy who wasn’t a star player or a famous coach. He walks us through the grind after getting let go at Wagner College — practicing every day at 40 until the calls started coming — and the lucky break that involved Jack Armstrong turning the job down and Mike Breen making a recommendation. 

Capstraw breaks down the craft of radio: the play-by-play guy paints the picture, the analyst “frames it and zings it,” and why it takes a long time to broadcast like yourself (his Miles Davis line). His favorite moment in broadcasting? The night he kept his mouth shut — silently writing “Pierce” so Chris Carrino could hit the legendary “Paul Pierce rejected!” call in Game 7 vs. Toronto.We also get into the beauty of the modern game’s chess match, why NBA coaches are “cream rises,” his love for Brook Lopez and Cam Johnson, and an honest Nets outlook: player development, Michael Brown’s “it factor,” Julius Randle and Michael Porter Jr., coach Jordy Fernandez, and the blunt rebuild truth — “We need a Jokić. We need a second-rounder that turns out to be the best player in the league.” 

Plus Brooklyn as the “third biggest city,” Barclays Center, and building culture while the Knicks own the championship glow.🏀 Subscribe to Hoopsology for smart, insider-level NBA and WNBA conversations every week.

episodes.title: Nuggets Shut Down Jokić Exit Rumors at Media Day
episodes.description:
The Denver Nuggets front office is not panicking — and they want you to know it. At the 2026 Nuggets Media Day, Ben Tenzer and Jonathan Wallace broke down the offseason, the Jokić contract situation, the Payton Watson trade, and what it will take to get back to the Finals.In this episode of the Hoopsology Podcast, we unpack everything they said. 

That starts with the biggest line of the day: on Nikola Jokić’s unsigned extension, the front office said they feel “very comfortable with the relationship, the trust there” and, flat out, “we have no concerns” — even if the team gets off to a bad start. They also explained why Josh Kroenke’s “everybody is on the table other than Nikola” comment did not turn into a teardown. After a 54-win season, they adjusted, liked the group, and chose not to overreact to the playoffs.

We cover the DeMar DeRozan addition (optionality, ball handling, veteran leadership, and “another level of culture”), the decision to trade Payton Watson for “very valuable draft capital” while firmly rejecting the idea that he quit on the team, and the plan for Aaron Gordon’s bounce-back season after front-office trips to Florida to support him and his family.Also: new medical staff (including a director of athletic training), earlier summer pickup, Cam Whitmore and Marvin Bagley joining a hungry bench, Coach Yeager and extra player-development coaches, Josh Kroenke managing culture day to day, and the West reality check — “we feel like we can compete with anybody,” with no magic shortcut back to the Finals except winning the day.

episodes.title: Clippers Scandal, Engelbert Exit & Steph's $116M Bet: Hoopsology ITL
episodes.description:
The NBA just hit the Los Angeles Clippers with one of the harshest punishments in league history. On this episode of the Hoopsology Podcast, Matt Thomas, Justin Goodrum and Alan Munzer break down everything: the $30 million fine, the loss of five first-round picks (2029–2033), Steve Ballmer's one-year suspension, Lawrence Frank's six-month suspension without pay, and Kawhi Leonard's $700,000 penalty.

Alan explains why he's called this a RICO case from day one, what the Eastern District of New York investigation could mean, and why he thinks Kawhi taking the deal "screwed the Clippers over one more time on his way out of town." We also ask the question every fan should be asking: which other front offices are cleaning their books right now?
Then we get into the WNBA's leadership shake-up. Cathy Engelbert is stepping down as WNBA commissioner. We weigh her business wins (team valuations averaging $460 million, record TV viewership, landmark media rights deals) against her strained relationships with players like A'ja Wilson and Caitlin Clark. Who should replace her? We debate Sue Bird, Swin Cash, Shareef Abdur-Rahim and NBA Deputy Commissioner Mark Tatum.

Plus: is Steph Curry's 2-year, $116 million extension a loyalty move or a real push to compete in the West? And our full WNBA playoff preview: Liberty vs Lynx, Mystics vs Dream, Wings vs Valkyries and Fever vs Aces. A healthy Caitlin Clark faces A'ja Wilson, the Valkyries bring elite defense, and Minnesota looks like a team of destiny.

episodes.title: Jokić on His Extension: "I'm Going to Sign Next Year… If They Want Me"
episodes.description:
Nikola Jokić is back, and he isn't holding back. At the 2026 Denver Nuggets Media Day, the three-time MVP talked about his contract extension, his legacy and what the Nuggets need to win another championship.In this episode of the Hoopsology Podcast, we break down everything Jokić said. That includes why he says delaying his extension was "entirely business," and his now-viral line: "I'm going to sign next year? If they want me." 

He also explained why staying with one team for his whole career matters so much to him. He remembers when there weren't many people in the stands, and now Denver has sold out more than 150 games in a row.

Jokić also made a bold point: every NBA player should play six months in Europe to feel the pressure of playing only to win. He looked back on captaining the Serbian national team, talked about getting over last season's playoff loss to Minnesota, and brushed off talk of a "body transformation" as normal yearly work.We also cover his big praise for Aaron Gordon ("there is no player in the league like him" when healthy), how new faces like DeMar DeRozan add new energy to the locker room, and whether this Nuggets roster can stay healthy enough to contend in the West.🏀 Subscribe to Hoopsology for smart, insider-level NBA and WNBA conversations every week.

We dive deep into what it really takes to be an NBA announcer: how Travis paints the picture so fans can see, smell, and feel the game, his game-day prep routine, how he handles shot-clock malfunctions and live improvisation, dealing with accusations of bias when you work for the team, and why storytelling and human connection matter more than stats.

Plus: why Rip City culture is truly unique — Portland as a one-sport town where the Trail Blazers are embedded in the fabric of the city, what makes Blazers fans the most rabid in the NBA, his take on last season's unpredictability, and his BOLD prediction for 45-50 wins and a top-six seed / play-in run.

episodes.title: Toronto Tempo's Wild Inaugural Season: Marina Mabrey's Redemption, Kiki Rice Rookie Year
episodes.description:
In this episode of the Hoopsology Podcast, we sit down with Savanna Hamilton — sports broadcaster and WNBA analyst covering the Toronto Tempo— to break down the Tempo's historic, and often chaotic, inaugural season in the WNBA.

Savanna takes us inside the year from the ground up: the surreal experience of documenting an expansion franchise's first season, the relentless injury bug that hit stars like Marina Mabrey, Nyara Sabally, and Kiki Rice, and how head coach Sandy Brondello's run-and-gun system has reshaped the roster around versatile players like Laura Juskaite. We dig into Marina Mabrey's incredible turnaround season — from her "crash out queen" reputation to an All-Star campaign capped by a 53-point outburst and MVP chants from the home crowd — and get an inside look at Kiki Rice's smooth rookie transition despite a shortened, CBA-delayed training camp.

Savanna also reflects on the emotional home opener in front of Toronto's first-ever WNBA crowd, what the team means for a new generation of Canadian fans, and how WNBA media coverage in Canada compares to the explosion of interest south of the border. Plus, she shares her take on the league-wide MVP race between Olivia Miles and A'ja Wilson, breaks down the playoff picture, and teases a big career announcement dropping this fall — including her role narrating the upcoming ESPN documentary on the Tempo's inaugural season.

episodes.title: "We Don't Want to Leave Anything on the Table" — The Lynx Are Done Waiting
episodes.description:
The Minnesota Lynx own one of the best records in the WNBA heading into the playoffs, and Star Tribune women's sports reporter Cassidy Hettesheimer joins Hoopsology to unpack exactly how they got here — and why anything short of a championship this year will feel like unfinished business.

Cassidy traces the season back to training camp, when even head coach Cheryl Reeve wasn't sure what to expect with Napheesa Collier sidelined recovering from double ankle surgery. What nobody fully anticipated was Olivia Miles: a rookie the coaching staff projected using full veteran statistical benchmarks rather than typical rookie expectations, who has since exceeded even that. Cassidy breaks down what makes Miles unique among a historically strong rookie class — a playmaking gift that makes everyone around her better, unlocking rim pressure the Lynx offense didn't have in years past — and shares a wonderfully human detail about Miles' transition to the league: figuring out where to sit at the team cafeteria table while simultaneously being trusted to direct All-Stars on the floor. Cassidy details the old-school, mentor-driven culture Cheryl Reeve has built around her, with veterans like Kayla McBride and Courtney Williams intentionally embracing and elevating their rookie floor general.

episodes.title: One Injury Changed Everything: How the Sparks' Season Fell Apart

The Los Angeles Sparks sit at 15-25, headed for a sixth straight season without a playoff appearance, and Hoopsology brings in Sparks beat writer John W. Davis (Southern California News Group) for an unflinching look at how a franchise with every natural advantage in the league ended up here.

John walks through the organizational chaos that's defined this stretch: four different head coaches since the drought began (Derek Fisher, interim Fred Williams, Curt Miller, and now Lynne Roberts), a revolving door of roster gambles that never got the runway to work, and a front office that kept trading the future for a present that never materialized — including dealing what became Dominique Malonga for Kelsey Plum after landing back-to-back No. 2 picks. He traces the fall from the Sparks' actual championship-caliber core of Candace Parker, Chelsea Gray, and Nneka Ogwumike, and explains why this season's collapse specifically comes down to one moment: Kelsey Plum, playing like a legitimate top-five player in the league, going down with an injury that the team simply had no answer for.

episodes.title: Marcus Thompson: The WNBA Legends We Let History Forget
episodes.description:
The Athletic's Marcus Thompson II joins Hoopsology to discuss his new book, "Game Changers: The GOATs Who Revolutionized Basketball," and delivers one of the most emotionally resonant conversations about the sport's history you'll hear this year.

Marcus explains how the book grew out of his 2021 book "Dynasties," where he realized basketball's greatest eras weren't siloed off from each other but deeply interconnected — you don't get the Warriors without Red Auerbach's Celtics first proving the value of getting from defense to offense faster. Applying that same "family tree" lens to individual players proved far harder, he admits, forcing him to build a strict rubric: not simply the best players, but the ones who fundamentally shifted how we think about the game. Steph Curry anchors that thesis — a player who averaged four threes a game as a rookie and normalized volume three-point shooting for everyone who came after him — but Marcus goes deeper, revealing the uncomfortable truth underneath most "revolutionary" moments: the resistance pioneers had to fight through.

Doug Feinberg, the Associated Press's national women's basketball writer, joins the Hoopsology Podcast to break down WNBA Commissioner Cathy Engelbert's surprise retirement announcement. Feinberg sat down with Engelbert directly and shares what her demeanor was really like, why she chose now to step away, and what she considers her biggest accomplishment after nearly seven and a half years leading the league.

We dig into the transformative CBA that delivered million-dollar player salaries and codified charter flights, whether Engelbert gets enough credit for getting that deal done, and how the media narrative around her tenure compares to what actually happened behind closed doors. Feinberg also compares her leadership style to Adam Silver's, addresses the manufactured controversy around league eligibility, and previews what the WNBA is looking for in its next commissioner — plus what's ahead with three new expansion franchises (Cleveland, Detroit, and Philadelphia) and the league's push to grow internationally.

episodes.title: How Former Players Actually Become NBA Coaches, Explained

After sharing a personal origin story rooted in a basketball-obsessed household and childhood trips to Georgetown basketball camps, the guest walks through nearly two decades working inside the NBA's player development and player engagement groups before taking on the CDP. They explain who's eligible (any former NBA, WNBA, G League, or even Basketball Africa League player), and walk through the full eight-month journey: a mostly virtual, Zoom-based curriculum focused on technology training, professional development like resume workshops and mock interviews, and hands-on shadowing opportunities at marquee basketball events throughout the year.

The conversation goes deep on what fans typically get wrong about the player-to-coach path — dispelling the myth that these hires either "come out of nowhere" or coast entirely on reputation — and unpacks the real, often-overlooked work: learning to self-advocate without an agent, building relationships, and getting comfortable walking up to strangers at industry events. The guest also details the specific software every candidate learns, including Synergy, Hudl SportsCode, and FastModel, and explains how those tools have transformed player evaluation, scouting reports, and in-game preparation compared to years past.

With more than 350 alumni to date — including names like Khalid El-Amin, Juan Dixon, Jawad Williams, Vin Baker, Nisha Curry, and Tamecka Dixon — the program has become a genuine pipeline into NBA, WNBA, and G League coaching staffs. In this clip from the Hoopsology Podcast, Front Office Sports reporter Colin Salao breaks down why the WNBA deleted its own post after promoting a betting moment between Paige Bueckers and Angel Reese, and why he believes this story has been dramatically underreported.

Colin walks through how the two stars were caught on video during an All-Star weekend practice at Chicago's Obama Center, casually agreeing to a $400 bet on an upcoming Wings-Dream matchup. The WNBA's own social media team later asked Bueckers on camera whether the bet still stood, compiled the footage, and posted it to the league's main account — before ultimately deleting it. Colin is careful to draw a distinction here: this wasn't a Terry Rozier-style scenario where a player is accused of manipulating a game's outcome for profit, but it was still players betting on their own league's games, which is explicitly prohibited under the CBA. He confirms that the WNBA ultimately announced no fines or penalties for Bueckers or Reese, while raising bigger questions about accountability for the social media team that posted it in the first place.

Colin's take is blunt: this is another example of the WNBA "shooting itself in the foot" — a self-inflicted controversy that got little mainstream coverage despite the obvious rule violation being promoted by the league's own channels.
